question: In July 2023 the Belarusian authorities amended the citizenship law to allow Belarusians living abroad charged with ‘participation in an extremist organisation’ or ‘grave harm to the interests of Belarus’ to be deprived of their citizenship. The measure also applies to Belarusians with no other citizenship.
Furthermore, the competences of consulates and diplomatic missions to issue, replace, or extend passports or identification cards of Belarusians abroad were abrogated in September 2023.

As a result, many exiled Belarusians, including members of the opposition, activists, human rights defenders, journalists and lawyers, currently fear statelessness or are forced to return to their home country, where they risk political prosecution and arbitrary arrest. 1.
What is the Commission doing to support Belarusians in exile who are being relentlessly targeted by the authorities?
Is there any citizenship programme the Commission could create to protect Belarusians who are at risk of statelessness?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.6.2024) The EU continues to follow closely the situation in Belarus and strongly condemns actions taken by the regime against exiled Belarusians.

The Commission would like to stress the vital importance of ensuring that Belarusian residents in the EU have access to identity and travel documents and have avenues of regularizing their stay despite not having access to consular services.

The Commission and the European External Action Service continue promoting exchanges with Member States on best practices at national level in order to find solutions for Belarusian citizens in the EU. It is important to note that third country nationals staying in the EU who cannot get a passport from their country of origin should primarily seek to get a travel document from the Member State they are resident in1.

Similarly, it is for each Member State, having due regard to international law, to lay down the conditions for acquisition and loss of nationality2. The Commission can thus not create a citizenship programme to protect Belarusians who are at risk of statelessness.

The EU reiterates its commitment to continue supporting people-to-people contacts, inter alia by supporting mobility, in line with the principles included in the Council Conclusions of 20203 and 20244.
1 Member States already issue passports and other identity documents to third country nationals that cannot

acquire those from their own government, according to national law. 2 See judgments of the Court of Justice of the European Union in Cases Micheletti and Others v Delegación del Gobierno en Cantabria, C-369/90, ECLI:EU:C:1992:295; Kaur, C-192/99, ECLI:EU:C:2001:106, para. 19; Rottmann, C-135/08, ECLI:EU:C:2010:104, para. 39; Tjebbes and Others, C-221/17, ECLI:EU:C:2019:189, para. 30; V.М.А.

, C-490/20, ECLI:EU:C:2021:1008, para. 38; Wiener Landesregierung, C-118/20, ECLI:EU:C:2022:34, para. 37. 3 Council conclusions on Belarus as adopted by the Council (Foreign Affairs) on 12 October 2020, https://www.consilium.europa.eu/media/46076/council-conclusions-on-belarus.pdf 4 Council conclusions on Belarus as approved by the Council (Foreign Affairs) on 19 February 2024, https://data.consilium.europa.
